title: Indus Valley Civilization
capsule: The Indus Valley Civilization (also called the Harappan Civilization) was a Bronze Age urban culture of the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra river systems that flourished c. 2600–1900 BC at its mature phase, encompassing more than 1,000 settlements including the twin metropolises of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each with populations estimated at 20,000–50,000. The civilization was notable for standardized weights and measures, a still-undeciphered script used on stamp seals, sophisticated municipal drainage systems, and remarkably uniform material culture across a territory larger than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. Urban decline began c. 1900 BC, associated with shifts in monsoon patterns and the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, and by c. 1700 BC most major urban centers had been abandoned or significantly reduced.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Indus Civilization's geographic extent is well attested archaeologically through site surveys; over 1,000 sites have been mapped from satellite imagery and ground surveys, though many peripheral sites remain unexcavated and the eastern boundary in Haryana and western boundary in Baluchistan carry uncertainty.
